{{short description|On decimal expansions of fractions with prime denominator and even repeat period}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Midy's theorem''', named after [[France|French]] [[mathematician]] E. Midy,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Leavitt|first=William G.|title=A Theorem on Repeating Decimals|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|date=June 1967|volume=74|issue=6|pages=669–673|url=http://digitalcommons.unl.edu/mathfacpub/48/|publisher=Mathematical Association of America|doi=10.2307/2314251|jstor=2314251|mr=0211949}}</ref> is a statement about the [[decimal expansion]] of [[Fraction (mathematics)|fraction]]s ''a''/''p'' where ''p'' is a [[prime number|prime]] and ''a''/''p'' has a [[repeating decimal]] expansion with an [[even number|even]] period {{OEIS|id=A028416}}. If the period of the decimal representation of ''a''/''p'' is 2''n'', so that

<math display=block>\frac{a}{p}=0.\overline{a_1a_2a_3\dots a_na_{n+1}\dots a_{2n}}</math>

then the digits in the second half of the repeating decimal period are the [[method of complements#Numeric complements|9s complement]] of the corresponding digits in its first half. In other words,

<math display=block>a_i+a_{i+n}=9 </math>
<math display=block>a_1\dots a_n+a_{n+1}\dots a_{2n}=10^n-1. </math>

For example,

<math display=block>\frac{1}{13}=0.\overline{076923}\text{ and }076+923=999. </math>
<math display=block>\frac{1}{17}=0.\overline{0588235294117647}\text{ and }05882352+94117647=99999999. </math>

==Extended Midy's theorem==   
If ''k'' is any [[divisor]] of ''h'' (where ''h'' is the number of digits of the period of the decimal expansion of ''a''/''p'' (where ''p'' is again a prime)), then Midy's theorem can be generalised as follows. The '''extended Midy's theorem'''<ref>Bassam Abdul-Baki, [http://www.abdulbaki.org/math/Midys_Theorem.pdf ''Extended Midy's Theorem''], 2005.</ref> states that if the repeating portion of the decimal expansion of ''a''/''p'' is divided into ''k''-digit numbers, then their sum is a multiple of 10<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1.

For example,   
<math display=block>\frac{1}{19}=0.\overline{052631578947368421} </math>   
has a period of 18. Dividing the repeating portion into 6-digit numbers and summing them gives   
<math display=block>052631+578947+368421=999999.</math>   
Similarly, dividing the repeating portion into 3-digit numbers and summing them gives   
<math display=block>052+631+578+947+368+421=2997=3\times999.</math>

==Midy's theorem in other bases==
Midy's theorem and its extension do not depend on special properties of the decimal expansion, but work equally well in any [[radix|base]] ''b'', provided we replace 10<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 with ''b''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 and carry out addition in base ''b''.

For example, in [[octal]]

<math display=block>
\begin{align}
& \frac{1}{19}=0.\overline{032745}_8 \\[8pt]
& 032_8+745_8=777_8 \\[8pt]
& 03_8+27_8+45_8=77_8.
\end{align}
</math>

In [[dozenal]] (using inverted two and three for ten and eleven, respectively)

: <math>
\begin{align}
& \frac{1}{19}=0.\overline{076\mathcal{E}45}_{12} \\[8pt]
& 076_{12}+\mathcal{E}45_{12}=\mathcal{EEE}_{12} \\[8pt]
& 07_{12}+6\mathcal{E}_{12}+45_{12}=\mathcal{EE}_{12}
\end{align}
</math>

==Proof of Midy's theorem==
Short proofs of Midy's theorem can be given using results from [[group theory]]. However, it is also possible to prove Midy's theorem using [[elementary algebra]] and [[modular arithmetic]]:

Let ''p'' be a prime and ''a''/''p'' be a fraction between 0 and 1. Suppose the expansion of ''a''/''p'' in base ''b'' has a period of ''ℓ'', so

<math display=block>
\begin{align}
& \frac{a}{p} = [0.\overline{a_1a_2\dots a_\ell}]_b \\[6pt]
& \Rightarrow\frac{a}{p}b^\ell = [a_1a_2\dots a_\ell.\overline{a_1a_2\dots a_\ell}]_b \\[6pt]
& \Rightarrow\frac{a}{p}b^\ell = N+[0.\overline{a_1a_2\dots a_\ell}]_b=N+\frac{a}{p} \\[6pt]
& \Rightarrow\frac{a}{p} = \frac{N}{b^\ell-1}
\end{align}
</math>

where ''N'' is the [[integer]] whose expansion in base ''b'' is the string ''a''<sub>1</sub>''a''<sub>2</sub>...''a''<sub>''ℓ''</sub>.

Note that ''b''<sup>&nbsp;''ℓ''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 is a multiple of ''p'' because (''b''<sup>&nbsp;''ℓ''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)''a''/''p'' is an integer. Also ''b''<sup>''n''</sup>&minus;1 is ''not'' a multiple of ''p'' for any value of ''n'' less than ''ℓ'', because otherwise the repeating period of ''a''/''p'' in base ''b'' would be less than ''ℓ''.

Now suppose that ''ℓ''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''hk''. Then ''b''<sup>&nbsp;''ℓ''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 is a multiple of ''b''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1. (To see this, substitute ''x'' for ''b''<sup>''k''</sup>; then ''b''<sup>''ℓ''</sup>&nbsp;=&nbsp;''x''<sup>''h''</sup> and ''x''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 is a factor of ''x''<sup>''h''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1. ) Say ''b''<sup>&nbsp;''ℓ''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 =&nbsp;''m''(''b''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1), so

<math display=block>\frac{a}{p}=\frac{N}{m(b^k-1)}.</math>

But ''b''<sup>&nbsp;''ℓ''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 is a multiple of ''p''; ''b''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 is ''not'' a multiple of ''p'' (because ''k'' is less than ''ℓ''&nbsp;); and ''p'' is a prime; so ''m'' must be a multiple of ''p'' and

<math display=block>\frac{am}{p}=\frac{N}{b^k-1}</math>

is an integer. In other words,

<math display=block>N\equiv0\pmod{b^k-1}. </math>

Now split the string ''a''<sub>1</sub>''a''<sub>2</sub>...''a''<sub>''ℓ''</sub> into ''h'' equal parts of length ''k'', and let these represent the integers ''N''<sub>0</sub>...''N''<sub>''h''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1</sub> in base ''b'', so that

<math display=block>
\begin{align}
N_{h-1} & = [a_1\dots a_k]_b \\
N_{h-2} & = [a_{k+1}\dots a_{2k}]_b \\
& {}\  \   \vdots \\
N_0 & = [a_{l-k+1}\dots a_l]_b
\end{align}
</math>

To prove Midy's extended theorem in base ''b'' we must show that the sum of the ''h'' integers ''N''<sub>''i''</sub> is a multiple of ''b''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1.

Since ''b''<sup>''k''</sup> is congruent to 1 modulo ''b''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1, any power of ''b''<sup>''k''</sup> will also be congruent to 1 modulo ''b''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1. So

<math display=block>N=\sum_{i=0}^{h-1}N_ib^{ik}=\sum_{i=0}^{h-1}N_i(b^{k})^i</math>
<math display=block>\Rightarrow N \equiv \sum_{i=0}^{h-1}N_i \pmod{b^k-1}</math>
<math display=block>\Rightarrow \sum_{i=0}^{h-1}N_i \equiv 0 \pmod{b^k-1}</math>

which proves Midy's extended theorem in base ''b''.

To prove the original Midy's theorem, take the special case where ''h'' = 2. Note that ''N''<sub>0</sub> and ''N''<sub>1</sub> are both represented by strings of ''k'' digits in base ''b'' so both satisfy

<math display=block>0 \leq N_i \leq b^k-1. </math>

''N''<sub>0</sub> and ''N''<sub>1</sub> cannot both equal 0 (otherwise ''a''/''p'' = 0) and cannot both equal ''b''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 (otherwise ''a''/''p'' = 1), so

<math display=block>0 < N_0+N_1 < 2(b^k-1) </math>

and since ''N''<sub>0</sub>&nbsp;+&nbsp;''N''<sub>1</sub> is a multiple of ''b''<sup>''k''</sup>&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1, it follows that

<math display=block>N_0+N_1 = b^k-1. </math>

==Corollary==
From the above,
<math display=block>\frac{am}{p}</math> is an integer

Thus <math>m \equiv 0 \pmod p</math>

And thus for <math>k = \frac{\ell}{2}</math>

<math display=block>b^{\ell/2}+ 1 \equiv 0 \pmod p </math>

For <math>k = \frac{\ell}{3}</math> and is an integer

<math display=block>b^{2\ell/3} + b^{\ell/3} + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod p </math>

and so on.
